rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Long-Term Memory (LTM) is the GCW's permanent knowledge store, encompassing all information the system has ever encountered or generated. It is a hybrid system that combines three types of memory: episodic, semantic, and procedural.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Episodic Memory stores complete records of the GCW's experiences – every task execution, every decision made, every success and failure, along with the full context (input state, reasoning steps, actions taken, outcomes). Each episode is stored as a node in the Knowledge Workspace, with rich metadata and a vector embedding that captures its semantic content. When the GCW faces a new task, it performs a similarity search on the episodic memory to retrieve past episodes that are analogous, enabling analogical reasoning and transfer learning. For example, if the GCW has previously written a successful grant proposal for a medical research project, and now it needs to write a proposal for a biotech project, it will retrieve that past episode and use it as a template, adapting the structure and phrasing to the new context. The system also performs episodic summarisation – a background process that identifies clusters of related episodes and generates higher-level summaries (e.g., "These 20 episodes all involve writing proposals for the NIH; the common success factors are X, Y, Z"). These summaries are stored as semantic memories.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Semantic Memory stores general knowledge, facts, concepts, and beliefs, derived from the user's input, the web, and the system's own inferences. This includes information from the Research Scientist's literature database, the Opportunity Discovery Engine's opportunity profiles, the Outreach Manager's contact profiles, and any user-provided documents. Semantic memories are stored as triples (subject, predicate, object) in a graph database (Neo4j), enabling complex relationship queries. For example, the system can query: "Find all projects related to 'cancer research' that were conducted in collaboration with 'Harvard University'". The graph is continuously updated as new information is acquired, and the system performs consistency checks to detect and resolve contradictions (e.g., if two sources state different publication dates for the same paper, the system flags this for user resolution).
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Procedural Memory stores skills – reusable sequences of actions that have been compiled into efficient routines. Skills are represented as Python functions (or, more generally, as executable scripts) that can be called by the GCW's reasoning engine. The skill library is initially seeded with a set of core skills (e.g., "send_email", "search_web", "write_code", "generate_document"), but new skills are continuously learned through a process of skill acquisition. When the GCW repeatedly performs a particular sequence of actions to achieve a specific goal, the system generalises that sequence into a new skill, parameterising it so it can be used in different contexts. The acquisition process uses a combination of pattern detection (identifying repeated action sequences in the action logs) and LLM-based generalisation (generating a generic description of the skill and its preconditions). Skills are stored in a dedicated skill repository, indexed by their purpose and preconditions, and they are versioned so that the GCW can revert to an older version if a new skill proves to be suboptimal.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 5.2.4 Deliberative Reasoning Engine – The Strategic Decision Maker
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The Deliberative Reasoning Engine is the "brain" of the GCW – the component that makes high-level strategic decisions, sets goals, decomposes complex problems, and chooses which actions to take. It is built around a hybrid architecture that combines a Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planner with a Large Language Model (LLM) that acts as a flexible, general-purpose reasoner.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The HTN planner is used for well-structured problems where the domain is known and the possible actions are well-defined. For example, planning a research project with a clear methodology, or planning an outreach campaign with a known sequence of steps. The HTN planner uses a library of "methods" – each method defines how to decompose a task into subtasks. For a novel task with no existing method, the system invokes the LLM to generate a new decomposition, which is then validated by the planner for consistency and feasibility, and if successful, the new method is added to the library for future use. This allows the system to continuously expand its planning capabilities.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The LLM-based reasoner is used for open-ended, ill-defined, or creative problems where the solution space is vast and not easily captured by a predefined method. The reasoner operates in a continuous loop of "sense-plan-act-reflect": it observes the current state (Working Memory), formulates a plan (a sequence of actions or sub-goals), executes the first action (via the Action Dispatcher), observes the result, and reflects on the outcome. The reflection step is crucial: it involves evaluating the success of the action, updating beliefs, and, if necessary, revising the plan. The reasoner uses a "scratchpad" – a temporary text document that records its chain-of-thought, alternative hypotheses, and decision rationales. This scratchpad is stored in Working Memory and can be reviewed by the user at any time. The reasoner is also capable of counterfactual reasoning – it can simulate alternative action sequences and evaluate their likely outcomes before committing to a plan, improving decision quality.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The reasoning engine also includes a meta-reasoning component that monitors the system's own reasoning processes. It tracks the time spent on each reasoning step, the confidence scores of the generated plans, and the success rate of past decisions. If the system detects that it is "stuck" (e.g., repeatedly generating similar plans that fail), it can initiate a meta-cognitive intervention, such as switching to a different reasoning strategy, requesting user input, or even pausing the task to focus on another project and returning with a fresh perspective.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 5.2.5 Action Dispatcher – The Physical Actuator
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The Action Dispatcher is the GCW's interface to the external world – it translates the reasoning engine's decisions into concrete actions that affect the digital environment. The dispatcher has access to a comprehensive registry of all available tools and services, including: all other Atlas AI modules (via their APIs), the Browser Agent for web interaction, a Python interpreter for code execution, the file system for reading and writing files, the email system for sending and receiving messages, and any third-party APIs that the user has configured. Each tool is described in a structured format (similar to OpenAI's function calling) that includes its name, a description, a list of parameters (with types and constraints), and any preconditions or side effects.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: When the reasoning engine decides on an action, it generates a "tool call" that specifies the tool name and the parameter values. The Action Dispatcher validates the call against the tool's schema, checks that all preconditions are met, and then executes the call. For tools that are other Atlas AI modules, the dispatcher makes a synchronous or asynchronous API call, depending on the expected duration. For long-running actions (e.g., "generate a 100-page report"), the dispatcher returns a task ID and the reasoning engine can continue with other work, periodically checking the task's status. For tools that involve external systems (e.g., "send an email"), the dispatcher handles authentication, rate limiting, and error handling, with retry logic and circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The Action Dispatcher also logs every action it performs, including the tool call, the parameters, the start and end times, and the result (success or failure, with any error messages). These logs are stored in the Knowledge Workspace as part of the episodic memory, providing a complete record of the GCW's activities.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 5.2.6 Meta-Cognitive Controller – Self-Awareness and Self-Regulation
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The Meta-Cognitive Controller is the GCW's "executive function" – the component that oversees the entire cognitive architecture, monitors its performance, and makes high-level adjustments to improve effectiveness. It is responsible for several key functions. First, resource allocation – it monitors the system's computational resources (CPU, memory, API credits, token budgets) and adjusts the reasoning engine's behaviour accordingly. For example, if the system is low on API credits, it may direct the reasoning engine to use cheaper models (like Llama locally) or to reduce the number of reasoning steps. Second, task prioritisation – it maintains a global task queue, prioritising tasks based on their urgency, the user's stated preferences, and the potential impact of the task. It can also preempt a low-priority task to allocate resources to a high-priority one. Third, error recovery – it monitors for failures in any of the system's components (e.g., an LLM call times out, a browser automation fails) and initiates a recovery procedure, which may involve retrying, switching to an alternative approach, or notifying the user. Fourth, skill acquisition – it identifies repetitive patterns in the system's actions and triggers the skill acquisition process to create new skills. Fifth, self-evaluation – it periodically reviews the GCW's overall performance, generating metrics such as task success rate, user satisfaction (inferred from approval rates and feedback), and efficiency (time and cost per task). It uses these metrics to suggest improvements to the system's configuration, such as adjusting the model router's thresholds or modifying the attention controller's parameters.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The Meta-Cognitive Controller is also responsible for maintaining the GCW's identity and persona. The system can be configured with a specific personality profile – for example, "formal and professional" for business contexts, or "creative and enthusiastic" for brainstorming sessions. The controller ensures that all generated communications and decisions are consistent with this persona, adjusting the tone, language, and even the types of suggestions the system makes.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 5.3 Operational Modes and Workflows
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The GCW can operate in three primary modes, depending on the user's needs and the nature of the task: Directed Mode, where the user provides explicit, detailed instructions; Autonomous Mode, where the GCW is given a high-level goal and is expected to figure out the best way to achieve it with minimal user interaction; and Collaborative Mode, where the system and user work together as partners, with the system making suggestions and the user providing feedback and guidance.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Directed Mode is used for tasks that are routine and well-understood, such as "Send an email to Professor Smith with the attached document". The GCW executes the task without any creative intervention, following the user's instructions precisely. This mode is efficient and minimises the risk of errors.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Autonomous Mode is the default mode for complex, long-duration projects. The user provides a goal, and the GCW takes full ownership of the project, decomposing it into subtasks, allocating resources, executing the subtasks, and reporting progress. The user can, at any time, intervene to provide additional guidance or to adjust priorities, but otherwise, the GCW operates independently. This mode is enabled by the system's robust planning, monitoring, and replanning capabilities.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Collaborative Mode is a more interactive style, where the GCW acts as a "thinking partner". It generates suggestions, raises questions, and presents alternative options, while the user provides judgments and direction. For example, when writing a grant proposal, the GCW might present three different narratives for the "Significance" section and ask the user to choose the most compelling one. This mode is useful when the task involves subjective decisions or when the user wants to retain a high level of control.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The GCW can transition seamlessly between these modes based on the task and the user's behaviour. For example, if the user starts providing very specific instructions, the system may switch to Directed Mode; if the user is silent for a while, it may switch to Autonomous Mode and continue working.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 5.4 Integration with Other Modules
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The GCW is not a standalone module; it is the orchestrator of the entire Atlas AI ecosystem. It integrates with all other modules through their APIs, invoking them as tools or sub-agents as needed. For example, when the GCW is working on a "research" project, it will call upon the Research Scientist module to perform literature reviews, the Browser Agent to search the web, the Document Generator to produce the final report, and the Email Assistant to communicate with collaborators. The GCW acts as the "manager" of these specialised modules, delegating tasks, monitoring their progress, and integrating their outputs.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The integration is facilitated by a unified messaging bus (Redis Streams) that allows the GCW to send commands to modules and receive events (progress updates, results, notifications) asynchronously. The GCW also maintains a shared state with the other modules through the Knowledge Workspace, ensuring that all modules have a consistent view of the current project status and data.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Goal Decomposition: The GCW's reasoning engine decomposes the high-level goal into three parallel workstreams: Market Analysis, Pitch Deck, and MVP Development. It estimates the effort required for each, assigns resources (dedicated sub-agents), and establishes a timeline with milestones. The plan is stored in the Knowledge Workspace and displayed on the Executive Dashboard.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Market Analysis Workstream: A sub-agent is spawned with the objective: "Conduct a comprehensive market analysis for a textbook rental platform in India." The sub-agent begins by invoking the Browser Agent to search for relevant market reports, competitor websites, and online discussions. It uses the Research Scientist module to find academic papers on the Indian education market. It also uses the Opportunity Discovery Engine to identify any existing platforms or similar startups. The sub-agent compiles the information, generates a SWOT analysis, estimates TAM/SAM/SOM, and creates a 15-page market report with charts and tables. The report is reviewed by the GCW's reasoning engine, which checks for completeness and consistency, and then it is presented to the user for feedback.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Pitch Deck Workstream: A second sub-agent is launched with the objective: "Create a compelling 10-slide pitch deck for a textbook rental platform." The sub-agent uses the market analysis report as input, extracting key points for each slide. It invokes the Document Generator to create the slides, using a pre-designed template optimised for venture capital presentations. It adds custom graphics (using matplotlib) for market size charts and financial projections. The draft deck is sent to the user for review, with a request for feedback on the narrative and design.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: MVP Development Workstream: A third sub-agent is initiated with the objective: "Build a functional MVP of the textbook rental platform." The sub-agent first generates a detailed technical specification, based on the market analysis and the user's initial description. It then invokes the Code Generation agent (via the AI Research Lab) to write the full-stack code: a Next.js frontend, a FastAPI backend, and a PostgreSQL database (with Supabase). The code is automatically tested using a suite of integration tests, and any failures trigger a self-healing loop. The MVP is deployed to a Vercel preview environment. The sub-agent also generates a set of user personas and simulates their interactions with the MVP, identifying usability issues and suggesting improvements.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Ongoing Monitoring and Coordination: Throughout the week, the GCW's Meta-Cognitive Controller monitors the progress of all three workstreams. Every morning at 9 AM, it generates a "stand-up" update, which is posted to the Executive Dashboard. The update summarises what was accomplished yesterday, what is planned for today, and any blockers. If a workstream is falling behind schedule, the controller can reallocate resources (e.g., assign more workers to that workstream) or adjust the plan. It can also proactively send questions to the user if it encounters an ambiguous requirement.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Final Deliverables: At the end of the week, the GCW compiles all outputs: the market analysis report, the pitch deck, and the MVP. It creates a final summary document that ties everything together. All deliverables are stored in the Knowledge Workspace and are accessible to the user through the Executive Dashboard. The user can then download them, share them with stakeholders, or continue working on the project with the GCW.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.source_text: 6.1 Security Architecture: Defense in Depth
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The security architecture of Atlas AI is built on the principle of defense-in-depth, with multiple layers of protection ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the system and its data. At the network level, all communication between services is encrypted using mutual TLS (mTLS), with each service possessing a unique certificate issued by an internal Certificate Authority. The certificates are automatically rotated every 24 hours to minimise the risk of compromise. The system is deployed in a private Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with strict network policies: only the API Gateway is exposed to the public internet, and all other services are only accessible within the VPC. The API Gateway itself is protected by a Web Application Firewall (WAF) that blocks common attack patterns such as SQL injection, XSS, and DDoS attempts.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Authentication and authorisation are handled by a dedicated Identity Provider (IdP) service that supports OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. Users can authenticate using their Google, GitHub, or custom credentials. Upon successful authentication, the user receives a JWT (JSON Web Token) that is used for subsequent API requests. The JWT has a short lifetime (15 minutes) and is refreshed using a long-lived refresh token. The system also supports multi-factor authentication (MFA) for enhanced security.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Sensitive data, such as API keys, database passwords, and user credentials, is stored in HashiCorp Vault. Vault is integrated with the system's deployment pipeline, and secrets are injected into the containers at runtime via environment variables or mounted volumes. No secrets are ever stored in the codebase or in plain-text configuration files. The system also encrypts all data at rest using AES-256, both in the databases (using PostgreSQL's TDE) and in cloud storage (using Google Cloud's server-side encryption). Additionally, any user data that is considered "highly sensitive" (e.g., financial information, health data) is encrypted at the application level before it is written to the database, using a per-user encryption key derived from the user's password (so that even the system administrators cannot decrypt it without the user's password).
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Audit logging is comprehensive and tamper-proof. Every action that modifies data or accesses sensitive information is logged to an append-only audit_log table. The log includes the user ID, the timestamp, the action type, the resource affected, and the IP address. The table uses a cryptographic hash chain: each row contains the SHA-256 hash of the previous row, ensuring that any modification to the log can be detected by recalculating the hashes. The audit logs are regularly backed up to a separate, immutable storage bucket.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 6.2 Observability: Comprehensive Monitoring and Diagnostics
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Observability is a first-class concern in Atlas AI, enabling the engineering team to understand the system's behaviour, diagnose issues, and optimise performance. The system uses OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing, with each service exporting traces to a central collector (Jaeger) that provides a unified view of request flows. Traces include detailed spans for each operation, with timing information and metadata. For example, a single API request that triggers a chain of Celery tasks and LLM calls will produce a trace that shows the latency of each step, helping to identify bottlenecks.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Structured logging is implemented across all services, with logs written to Google Cloud Logging. The logs are enriched with a common set of fields: trace_id, span_id, service_name, user_id (if available), and severity. This allows for efficient filtering and correlation. The system also generates custom metrics, which are exposed via the Prometheus endpoint and visualised in Grafana dashboards. Key metrics include: request rate and latency per API endpoint, task queue length, LLM call latency and token usage, error rates, and resource utilisation (CPU, memory). Alerting rules are defined for critical metrics, such as "error rate > 5% for 5 minutes" or "task queue length > 1000", triggering notifications via email, Slack, or PagerDuty.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system also includes an anomaly detection module that uses machine learning (a combination of statistical models and neural networks) to automatically detect unusual patterns in the metrics and logs. For example, it can detect a sudden drop in the success rate of a particular module, or a gradual degradation in the performance of a specific LLM. These anomalies are flagged for investigation, and the system can automatically take corrective actions (e.g., rolling back a recent deployment, switching to a backup model) if the anomaly is severe.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: 6.3 Cost Management: Financial Governance and Optimisation
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Cost management is critical, especially given the heavy reliance on external LLM APIs. The system maintains a comprehensive cost tracking mechanism that records every LLM call, including the model used, the number of input and output tokens, and the cost per token (based on the current pricing). The costs are aggregated by module, by user, and by project, and they are displayed in a dedicated "Cost Dashboard" in the Executive Dashboard. The dashboard shows daily, weekly, and monthly trends, and allows users to set budget alerts.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system also implements cost optimisation strategies. The model router (Module 12) is cost-aware, and it can dynamically choose cheaper models if the task's quality requirements are low. The system also uses caching for frequent queries: if the same query is repeated within a certain time window, the system returns the cached response instead of making a new LLM call. Additionally, the system can batch requests: when multiple tasks require similar LLM processing, they can be batched into a single call to the API, reducing the per-request overhead.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system also supports cost forecasting, using historical data to predict future spending and notify the user if the projected spending exceeds the budget. This allows the user to adjust their usage or allocate more funds proactively.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.source_text: 6.4 Multi-Tenancy: Scalable User Support
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: While Atlas AI is primarily designed for individual users, the architecture is multi-tenant ready. The database schema includes a tenant_id column in all tables, and all queries are automatically filtered by the tenant ID (via Row Level Security in PostgreSQL). The system uses a separate database schema for each tenant, providing strong isolation. The API Gateway verifies that the user's JWT contains the correct tenant ID, ensuring that a user cannot access another tenant's data. The system also supports single sign-on (SSO) across multiple tenants, allowing users with accounts in multiple tenants to switch seamlessly.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: For future scaling, the system is designed to support sharding by tenant, with each tenant's data stored in a separate database cluster. The system uses a sharding key (the tenant ID) to route requests to the appropriate cluster, and the sharding strategy can be changed dynamically.
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.source_text: The entire Atlas AI system is containerised using Docker, with multi-stage builds that optimise the image sizes. Each service has its own Dockerfile, and the images are stored in a private container registry (Google Container Registry). For local development, Docker Compose is used to spin up the entire stack (including PostgreSQL, Redis, ChromaDB, and all services) with a single command.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: For production, the system is deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Kubernetes manifests define the deployments, services, ingress, and ConfigMaps for each component. The system uses Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) to scale the stateless services (like the API Gateway and the Celery workers) based on CPU utilisation and custom metrics (like the length of the Celery queue). The databases are managed services (Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, Memorystore for Redis) to reduce operational overhead.

rows.source_text: 7.2 CI/CD Pipeline
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system uses a continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline built on GitHub Actions. The pipeline is triggered on every push to the main branch. It runs a comprehensive suite of tests: unit tests (for each service), integration tests (testing the interactions between services), and end-to-end tests (testing the full system from the user's perspective). The tests are run in a isolated environment to prevent interference. If all tests pass, the pipeline builds the Docker images, tags them with the commit hash, and pushes them to the container registry. The deployment step then applies the Kubernetes manifests to the staging environment, runs a suite of smoke tests, and, if they pass, promotes the deployment to the production environment using a blue-green deployment strategy to minimise downtime.

rows.source_text: 7.3 Scalability Considerations
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Scalability is addressed at multiple levels. The stateless services (API Gateway, Celery workers) can be scaled horizontally by increasing the number of replicas. The stateful services (PostgreSQL, Redis) are scaled vertically (by increasing the instance size) or horizontally (by using read replicas for PostgreSQL and Redis Cluster for Redis). The AI Research Lab uses a dedicated queue for LLM calls, ensuring that high-priority tasks are not blocked by low-priority ones.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system is designed to handle bursts of traffic. For example, when a large batch of opportunities is discovered, the system can process them in parallel by increasing the number of Celery workers. The system also supports priority queuing: tasks from the Approval Center have the highest priority, followed by tasks from the Planner, and then background tasks.

rows.source_text: 7.4 Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system has a comprehensive disaster recovery plan. The databases are backed up continuously (point-in-time recovery is enabled for PostgreSQL). The backups are stored in a different geographic region to protect against regional failures. In the event of a complete failure of the primary region, the system can be restored in the backup region within a few hours. The system also supports chaos engineering – it runs regular tests where it randomly kills services or introduces network latency to ensure that the system is resilient to failures.

rows.source_text: 8. Future Evolution and Continuous Improvement
rows.notes: Requires atomic decomposition and behavior evidence before status can change.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: Atlas AI is not a static system; it is designed for continuous evolution. The architecture is modular, allowing for easy replacement of components. The AI Research Lab can integrate new models as they become available. The Planner and the GCW's reasoning engine can be updated with new algorithms. The system uses A/B testing to evaluate new features: a subset of users is given access to a new feature, and their behaviour is compared to a control group to determine if the feature improves metrics (e.g., user satisfaction, task completion rate).

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The system also includes a feedback loop where user interactions are logged and analysed. This analysis identifies common pain points, missing features, and opportunities for improvement. The system can also automatically generate "bug reports" when it detects unusual behaviour (e.g., an LLM call that produced a response that is inconsistent with the input). These reports help the engineering team prioritise fixes.

rows.module: Part 5 – Module 20: General Cognitive Worker (Universal Intellectual Agent) – Complete Technical Specification
rows.source_text: The long-term roadmap for Atlas AI includes: integrating with more external data sources and APIs, adding support for more languages and cultures, enhancing the GCW's creative capabilities (e.g., generating music or art), and enabling the system to work with physical devices (via IoT integration). The system is also being designed to support collaborative multi-user projects, where multiple users can work together with the GCW on the same project.
